cards.text: A picture gets stronger when it has more to hold on to. Try adding one sense besides sight. For bread, hear the crust crackle and feel the heat on your palms. Each extra detail is one more thing that might bring the picture back. This is about the item, not about you: use whichever sense gives the richest picture for the thing in front of you.

Over the year you will meet many methods. Try each one on your own material and keep the ones that work for you. Your own scores will tell you, though a few attempts is not much to go on. We do not sort anyone into types: careful reviews of the research found no good evidence that people learn better when material is taught in their preferred style.

A shopping list makes a good first chain. Take eggs, soap, plums and rope. The eggs crack open over a bar of soap, the soap slides into a bowl of plums, and the plums are tied up with the rope. Say the story once in your head, then once more, slowly. Write the list down too when missing something would matter: the story is your second copy, not your only one.

A short routine is just a list with an order, so a chain works for it. Give each step one keyword, the thing you will see in your mind. For making tea: kettle, pot, leaves, pour, wait, strain. The kettle fills the pot, the pot tips out the leaves, the leaves are poured on by a waterfall, and so on. The chain keeps the order of the steps. It cannot teach you the skill, and for anything where a slip could cause harm, keep the written steps in front of you.

A palace does not have to be a whole house. One room is enough, and in Mnemos a palace of one room is called a Roman Room. Ordered-place methods are described in old Roman writing on public speaking, so the idea is a very old one. Stand at the door and walk the walls in a fixed direction: door, wall hook, window, shelf, bed, wardrobe. Eight to twelve stops is plenty. A single room holds a short list well, and a long list needs more rooms.

Try a grocery list in your palace. Put one item at each stop and let it do something to the spot: a melon rolling off the hall table, a tub of butter melting down the coat hook. If you like, place the items in the order you will pass the aisles, so the walk in your head matches the walk in the shop. A palace stores the list; check your written list at the shop door before you leave.

A journey is a palace made from a walk you know, like your walk to the bus or your route to the shop. Each landmark is a stop: corner shop, bus stop, bridge, post box, park gate, bench. Choose landmarks that are clearly different and a few steps apart. One landmark gets one picture, and two doors side by side get mixed up. A room, a gallery and a journey are the same method at different sizes.

Before the Major code, there is a simpler image method for single digits: give each digit a picture shaped like it. 1 is a candle, 2 is a swan, 3 is a pair of handcuffs. The digits 3, 1, 2 become handcuffs round a candle, with a swan sitting on top. You will meet all ten shape pictures in week 24. This works for a digit or two. For long numbers the Major System is the better fit, because one picture stands for two digits, which is why you are learning it now.

Your list of pictures for 00 to 99 is your own image library, and it is yours to shape. Many people find a picture from their own life easier to find again than a stock one: for 21, which is n and t, use the fishing net from your uncle's boat rather than any net. Pick one picture per number and keep it. Changing a picture halfway through costs more than keeping a slightly weaker one. A library takes repeated use before it feels automatic.

Chunking means gathering small pieces into one bigger unit that you hold as a single thing. A phone number is written 482 915 603 and not 482915603 for this reason. The Major System already chunks for you: two digits turn into one picture. Psychologists have argued about how many chunks a person can hold at once, from about seven down to about four, so there is no magic number. Find the group size that works for you and stay with it.

Try saying a number aloud in a beat. Take 482 915 603 774 and say it as four groups of three, with a small pause after each group and the stress on the first digit of the group. The beat may give you one more thing to hold on to when you recall. Saying things aloud has been found to help memory a little. Whether a beat adds anything on top of that is only a guess. Do this away from the drill screen, because the game stays quiet while you study and recall. It is a modest help at most, not a trick.

Many abstract words sound like something you can see. Peace sounds like piece, so picture a piece of pie held out in an open hand. Words that sound the same but are spelled and meant differently, like peace and piece, are called homophones. Others only sound close, like hope and hoop: picture a hoop you are about to jump through. Either kind makes a handy stand-in. As with any keyword, the picture gets the word in quickly and fades unless you check it again, which is why the app brings it back later.

A Mind Map is a drawing of how a topic fits together. The topic sits in the middle. Main branches leave it, and short leaves hang from each branch. For the planets: Planets in the centre, then three branches, Rocky (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars), Gas giants (Jupiter, Saturn) and Ice giants (Uranus, Neptune). On paper, use a big sheet, one word or two per leaf, and keep it plain.

An honest word about maps. The drawing shows how a topic fits together. What helps memory most is closing it and rebuilding it from nothing. In one well-known experiment, students who practised recalling a text remembered more a week later than students who built a concept map while studying it. Reviews of many studies find that studying or making maps helps on average, with large differences from study to study. So in Mnemos you study the map, then it disappears and you rebuild it.

Do not memorise a talk word for word. Cut it into five to nine points and give each point one keyword, the first thing you need to say. A talk about opening a community garden might run: why (seed), where (map), who helps (glove), tools (spade), dates (calendar), costs (coin), thanks (flower). Place the seven keywords along your route. The route keeps your order. It does not write the talk, so rehearse the words out loud as well.

For a job interview, prepare three short stories about your work: a problem you solved, a time you worked with others, a time you learned something. Add the interviewer's name and your own two or three questions to ask. Put the three stories first in a six-stop Roman Room, then the name, then the questions, so you can scan them in order while you wait. Preparation can help you keep your points in order. It does not decide how an interview goes, and it is fine to bring notes if they are allowed.

Five rules for a good map. One: put the topic in the middle in a few words. Two: use three to six main branches, each with a clear label. Three: give each branch two to four leaves, and keep each leaf to one to three words. Four: make the branches the same kind of thing, such as when, where and who, so each leaf knows where it belongs. Five: close it, rebuild it blank, and fix only what you missed.

Here is a map of an invented person, Tomas Wrenfield. Branches: Home (Oakhallow, a grey cat), Born (9 March), Fun (kite flying, a green van) and Food (lentil soup, pear cake). When you rebuild it, say the person first, then each branch, then the leaves. In real life, map only what people are happy for you to remember, and keep private details out of any notes you share.

Now a map of a subject: the planets again, but with a picture on each branch. Rocky gets a lump of brick, Gas giants get a big balloon and Ice giants get a block of ice. Put each of the three pictures at a stop. Walk the stops, and let each picture bring back its leaves. Study the map, close it, rebuild it. The rebuilding is the part that helps.

Here is a three-step habit to get the most from every check. Close the notes. Say or write everything you can recall, even the parts you are unsure of. Then open the notes and check, marking only what you missed. Pulling something out of memory is slower than reading it again, and that effort is thought to be part of why it lasts longer. Repeat the check after a gap of a day, then a week, and spread out your checks over time.

Skim, Pick, Keep is a three-step habit for a text you must remember. Skim: spend a short time on the headings and the first and last line of each part. Pick: choose five to nine key points. Keep: give each point one picture and one place, and check yourself later. For a leaflet about a community garden, the headings might be Plots, Tools, Water and Rules, and each heading gets one picked point and one keyword.

Skimming is a reading strategy. It finds the key points, and it does not store them. Keeping them is a separate job: a picture, a place and a check later. Reading faster tends to cost understanding, so skim when you need the shape of a text and read slowly when understanding matters. The pictures in Mnemos help with lists, names and exact wording, not with understanding an argument.

A routine procedure is a chain with a keyword per step. For repotting a houseplant: pot, soil, roots, press, water. Link the five keywords, or place them on five stops. Read the instructions with care first, and check your memory against them afterwards. A chain keeps the order of steps. It does not teach you why each step matters, and where a slip could hurt someone you should always keep the written steps in front of you.

Make this your keeping habit: check before you look. When you review a palace, a list or a page of notes, try to recall it first, and then open your copy and mark the gaps. A short regular check is better than one long session. If you reread without trying first, it feels easy and teaches less.

For a work presentation, use a Roman Room you know well, like the meeting room or your desk. Five points on five stops: door, table, screen, window, chair. Rehearse out loud at least twice, because walking the points is not the same as saying them. Keep a one-page Mind Map in your bag as a second copy. A tidy route helps you keep the order. It does not make the talk good.

week24: A peg is a fixed hook that you know by number. Learn a short row of ten pegs by heart, then hang any list on them, one item per peg. Because each peg has a number, you can ask for number 7 straight away, without walking through the first six. There are two kinds, shape pegs and rhyme pegs, and you can use either or both.

Shape pegs look like their number: 1 candle, 2 swan, 3 handcuffs, 4 sailboat, 5 hook, 6 golf club, 7 cliff edge, 8 snowman, 9 balloon on a string, 10 bat and ball. To remember milk, bell, fish and kite: a milk carton burns like a wick on the candle, a bell hangs round the swan's neck, a fish is caught in the handcuffs, and a kite is the sail of the sailboat. To recall, count from one and see what is attached to each shape.

Rhyme pegs sound like their number: 1 bun, 2 glue, 3 tree, 4 oar, 5 beehive, 6 sticks, 7 heaven (a bright cloud), 8 crate, 9 vine, 10 hen. To remember stamp, lamp and rope in slots 1 to 3: a stamp squashes a bun flat, a lamp is stuck fast in a pool of glue, and a rope is slung over a tree. The sound gives you a second route from the number to the picture, so if the shape does not come, the rhyme may.

Which should you use, pegs or a palace? Pegs suit short lists of ten or so, especially when someone may ask for a number out of order. A palace suits long lists and lists you will keep. Peg lists get used again and again, so a new list can blur into the last one. Wait a day between lists, or switch between the shape list and the rhyme list. Each is a tool, and neither is the best for everything.
